The integrated approach is currently being successfully applied to small satellite missions and systems design, covering a wide variety of mission concepts from LEO Earth Observation missions to close-proximity operations missions, up to deep-space missions, with a focus to the CubeSat platform.

To support this extension of applicability, a critical challenge of the concurrent design approach needs first to be overcome: the seamless integration across organizational borders due to both technical limitations in data exchange systems and the inherent complexity of space systems. Achieving full compatibility between diverse systems and real-time data synchronization remains difficult, primarily due to tool, standard, and process variations across different partners.

By combining these methodologies, we propose an integrated and agile approach that maintains a single source of truth, ensures continuity of information across the mission lifecycle, and facilitates collaboration among engineering teams and stakeholders.

This methodology demonstrates how CE, when combined with MBSE and DDSE, can optimize space mission design from concept to manufacturing and testing up to in-orbit operations and disposal, providing a robust solution for small satellite and space systems development.

Its main advantages include consistency, automation, and transparency, while key limitations are its critical dependence on data accuracy, high infrastructure costs, and the risk of information overload if data governance is insufficient.

MBSE is recognised for its strengths in complexity management, requirements traceability, and communication across disciplines. However, it requires substantial training, tool investments, and still suffers from a lack of standardisation across industrial applications [8].

The methodology is based on the integration of two open and widely adopted tools: Valispace, which embodies the DDSE philosophy by managing engineering data within a single source of truth; and Capella, which implements the ARCADIA method to provide structured, model-based representations of system architecture and behaviour [6].

In this approach, Capella is designated as the master environment for mission and system architectures, functional analysis, and operational scenarios, while Valispace serves as the supporting environment for requirements management, parametric budgets (e.g., mass, power, volume), and trade-off analysis.

Information continuity is ensured by synchronisation scripts developed in Python. These scripts exploit the Capella add-on Python for Capella and the Valispace REST API to extract functions, logical components, and operative modes from Capella and import them into Valispace, while preserving hierarchy and consistency.

Conversely, Valispace supports the Capella models with concrete engineering data, enabling simulations and trade-offs. This bidirectional workflow guarantees digital continuity and the preservation of a single authoritative dataset throughout the design process.
Together, they form a comprehensive framework capable of supporting the entire lifecycle of small-satellite missions.

Clients and decision-makers can follow the Capella models to understand high-level architecture and operational scenarios, while engineers rely on Valispace to assess the quantitative implications of design changes.

Early stakeholder analysis and ConOps modelling: Initial mission and customer needs are identified and defined as requirements on Valispace. Then, the stakeholder needs analysis is conducted on Capella, where it is executed more successfully. Another feature offered by Capella is the definition of the Concept of Operations (ConOps), exploiting the VPMS add-on, which offers the capability to create the Configurations.
Hierarchy preservation: Logical and physical component trees are synchronised across tools using dedicated scripts, maintaining coherence between system models and data repositories.
Mode-based budgeting: Operative modes defined in Capella are transferred into Valispace, where they support dynamic budget estimations (e.g., power consumption per mode).

Automated verification and trade-offs: Through Valispace, budgets are automatically checked against requirements, enabling rapid trade-off studies (e.g., battery sizing) that are immediately consistent with the architectural model.
It provides a scalable methodology that ensures transparency, traceability, and efficiency throughout the system lifecycle, paving the way for more agile and reliable satellite mission design.

"The mission shall act as a technology demonstrator in LEO for deep-space small satellites, focusing on navigation, communication and operations technologies, while simultaneously monitoring environmental parameters to characterise the UHI effect in urban areas."

The process began with a systematic stakeholder needs analysis, using Capella's Operational Analysis (OA) level. Stakeholders included ESA (interested in deep-space technology validation and UHI complementarity with Copernicus services), research institutions, the space industry (seeking to raise Technology readiness Level (TRL) of components), and end-users such as governments, environmental organisations and energy providers.

Operational Capabilities Blank (OCB) and Operational Architecture Blank (OAB) diagrams (figures 3 and 4) were created in Capella to capture stakeholder objectives and the interactions between entities. These outputs were then translated into high-level requirements in Valispace, ensuring consistency between the stakeholder view and engineering data.

Functions were broken down into sub-functions and allocated to logical components. Scripts exported these elements and imported them into Valispace, where they became linked requirements and system components, preserving hierarchy, traceability and conformity between the two tools.
These actors defined in Capella were subsequently imported as Components into Valispace thanks to a Python parser, to ensure consistency between the two tools at an early stage (figure 6).

Once it was clear all the actors involved and their interaction with the system, based on the knowledge and considerations from the Operational level, a functional analysis was performed. The identified functions were allocated to the SoI and/or the actors, and functional and component exchanges were identified to get a complete picture of the high-level functions needed to satisfy the mission itself.

The ConOps included Integration & Testing (I&T), Launch and Early Orbit Phase (LEOP), the Operative Phase and End of Life (EOL). In particular, the Operational Phase consisted of two distinct subphases.

Once the preliminary functional analysis was conducted on Capella, new mission requirements were updated on Valispace. By employing the Python scripts, Capella's functions of interest could be imported into Valispace as new requirements.
System functions were broken down into sub-functions, and the system was broken down into logical components, as shown in figure 8.
Scripts exported these elements and imported them into Valispace, where logical functions and components became respectively linked requirements and subsystem components, maintaining their hierarchy.

Subsequently, a "bridge" Python script was exploited to involve both tools simultaneously and to verify their compliance in terms of the product tree. The figure 10 shows the output that the code displays in the console when a component apperas to be absent on Valispace. Furthermore, given the adoption of Capella as a master tool, the code automatically updated the component structure in Valispace, restoring conformity between the two.
Following the identification of new components and functions, the logical architecture was modelled, which is the result of design choices and decisions involving all the subsystems.

Another feature that was exploited on Capella is the use of the Modes and States Diagrams (MSM) diagrams to define the operative modes and their triggers, with the purpose of supporting the deep-space demonstration for the autonomous operations. These were subsequently imported into Valispace as Modelists, and associated with the Space Segment and the different subsystems through the use of Python scripts.

Although the operative modes were significantly clearer on Capella, the process of importing them into Valispace allowed us to exploit its budget estimation capacity. The creation of a "Power" matrix depending on the operative mode (figure 11) enabled the tool to automatically compute a power budget.
The work started on the Physical Architecture level on Capella with the definition of the concrete physical components of each subsystem.

In Valispace, detailed subsystem design and trade-offs were carried out using imported physical components and associated engineering parameters. For example, a battery trade-off was performed by defining multiple design alternatives, with automatic propagation of impacts on the spacecraft power budget (Figure 13). This ensured that design choices remained consistent with the architectural constraints defined on Capella.
Firstly, continuity of information is highlighted, as requirements, architectures, and budgets were synchronised across tools, reducing inconsistencies.
Additionally faster iterations were possible, mainly because changes in one domain (e.g., subsystem sizing)
were immediately propagated to others, accelerating design convergence.
A key aspect was the transparency and traceability, where stakeholders could follow both functional models (Capella) and quantitative budgets (Valispace), fostering clearer decision-making.
Finally, automated budget updates allowed efficient evaluation of design alternatives under real mission constraints, efficiently supporting trade-offs.

Overall, the GeoProfundo mission validated the applicability of the Concurrent Data-Driven Model-Based framework to small-satellite design, illustrating its capacity to support multidisciplinary teams, enhance transparency, and improve efficiency during early lifecycle phases.
Combined with CE, this integration demonstrated how task parallelization across disciplines allows for the immediate evaluation of design trade-offs, thereby reducing both development time and costs.

Capella proved particularly effective for defining and developing system and subsystem architectures, offering a structured model-based framework well-suited to the management of system complexity. In parallel, Valispace supported the real-time management of requirements and engineering data.
The methodology proved effective as a foundation for more detailed design activities and shows strong potential for extension to Assembly, Integration, Verification and Testing (AIV/T) management.

The interoperability between Capella and Valispace, enabled through Pythonbased scripting, further reinforces this complementarity and remains adaptable even for users with limited programming expertise.
Future work will focus on the development of a dedicated graphical user interface to simplify tool integration and facilitate wider adoption of the Concurrent Engineering paradigm.
